Clinical Neuropathology, Vol. 16, No. 4 — 1997 (214-219)
Stiff-man syndrome: possible autoimmune
etiology targeted against GABA-ergic cells
2 1 1
M. Waricu-Kircues", P. Von Bossanyt', T. Treunelt’, E. Kircues , K. DIETZMANN ,
2 1
H. FetstNerTM and H. Wittic
‘Department of Neuropathology, and "Department of Neurophysiology, Medical School,
Otto-von-Guericke University, Magdeburg, Germany
Abstract. We report the case of a female patient, who died at the age of 66 years. Besides an
insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM) she had developed the clinical symptoms of stiff-man-
syndrome (SMS) and harbored autoantibodies against glutamate-decarboxylase (GAD) in blood and
liquor. GAD catalyzes the biosynthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter y-aminobutyric acid
(GABA). The autopsy revealed typical alterations observed in diabetes mellitus including an incom-
plete fibrosis of pancreatic Langerhans islets. A decrease of GABA-ergic cells in the cerebellar cortex
was observed, and a size reduction of Renshaw cells in the spinal cord. Furthermore, a dilution series
of a polyclonal GABA antibody delivered a reduced immunofluorescence in the cerebellum. In
skeletal muscle a neurogenic atrophy was observed. As described in literature, the clinical symptoms
decayed following clonazepam administration. We suggest that this case including GAD autoanti-
bodies, dramatic loss of GAD-expressing pancreatic cells, and loss or atrophy of GABA secretory
neurons, supports the hypothesis that SMS may be an autoimmune disease directed against GABA-
ergic cells. Furthermore, we suggest a neuronal hypersensitivity at the spinal cord level caused by the
atrophic Renshaw cells.
Key words: stiff-man-syndrome - GABA — GAD — IDDM — autoimmune disease
Introduction
SMS is a rare CNS disease characterized by rigidity
and painful spasms of the musculature. There are many
Open questions concerning pathogenesis and etiology
[Spada and Spada 1994]. While in adults it is a sporadic
disease, the congenital variant is inherited as an autosomal
dominant trait [Pongratz et al. 1990]. Since GAD autoan-
tibodies were observed frequently, some authors suggest a
neuronal autoimmune disease [Giometto et al. 1994, Pon-
gratz et al. 1990, Seitz et al. 1995, Spada and Spada 1994].
GAD catalyzes the biosynthesis of the inhibitory neuro-
transmitter GABA. The first step of the pathway takes
place in the mitochondria of the axon terminals generating
the product glutamate. In the cytoplasm GAD converts
glutamate into free cytosolic GABA. Enclosed in mem-
brane vesicles GABA can be transported to the presynaptic
membrane and is released into the synaptic cleft following

neuronal activation. It can be bound by receptors in the
postsynaptic membrane [Leonhardt et al. 1987]. In addi-
tion, GABA may leave the neuron by other mechanisms.
It may be trapped by astrocytes which reconvert it into
glutamate. GAD is the key enzyme of GABA biosynthesis.
The presence of the enzyme within a cell clearly indicates
its GABA-ergic function [Leonhardt et al. 1987]. One
aspect of the pathogenesis may be that the loss of GABA
secretory neurons or their impaired function, caused by an
autoimmune disease, leads to an insufficient down-regula-

tion of spinal inhibitory routes, which are responsible for
the relaxation of muscle tension and extroceptive spinal
reflexes [Pongratz et al. 1990]. Furthermore, GAD autoan-
tibodies were sometimes detected in insulin-dependent
diabetes mellitus [Nathan et al. 1995] and an association of
both diseases was suggested [Pugliese et al. 1994, Soli-
mena et al. 1988]. On the other hand, Schmidt et al. [1975]
assume that SMS is based upon a disturbed norepinephrine
system exhibiting an excitatory effect on motor neurons.
To further elucidate the pathogenetical and structural
alterations of this rare disease we want to present this new
case. Our special interest was focused on the qualitative
and quantitative alterations of GABA- and GAD-rich cells
in brain, spinal cord, and pancreas.

Methods
Immunohistochemistry
Small pieces of autoptic material (1.5 x 0.5 x 1 cm)
were fixed for 2 days and complete brains for a period of
4 weeks in 5% formalin. Following paraffin embedding,
slices of 4, 7, 15, and 20 um, respectively, were stained
with a hematoxyline/eosine (HE), Berlin blue, trichrome,
Nissl, Glia, Bodian, and silver stain for Schwann cells.
In the patient and a control, cerebellum as well as
Renshaw cells and GABA-rich neurons of Deiter’s nucleus
were Stained with a rabbit polyclonal GABA antibody
(Sigma, USA) and secondary detection was performed
using the Extra Avidin kit (Sigma, USA). In brief, 4 um
thick sections were dewaxed and treated with 0.3% hydro-
gen peroxide in methanol followed by an incubation in
10% normal goat serum. The slices were treated with
primary antibody (diluted 1 : 200 in PBS) at 37° C for 1
hour. Following PBS washes, they were incubated with
biotinylated anti-rabbit IgG and developed with avidin
peroxidase. The peroxidase reaction was visualized with
diaminobenzidine/hydrogen peroxide. PBS was used in
place of primary antibody for negative controls.
To elucidate the influence of SMS on GABA-ergic
neurons of the cerebellar cortex, slices were stained with
fluorescence-labeled antibodies. For this purpose 6 um
cryostat sections were dried at room temperature for 24
hours, fixed in acetone, and air-dried. They were treated
with 0.3% hydrogen peroxide, followed by 10% normal
goat serum. Afterwards, the slices were incubated for 60
minutes at 37° C with a polyclonal GABA antibody, di-
luted 1 : 100, 1 : 200, 1 : 300, 1 : 400 and 1 : 500 in PBS.
Following PBS washes, the sections were treated with
TRITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Sigma, USA) di-
luted 1 : 30 (30 minutes, 37°C). A cooled slow-scan CCD
camera (CF 20 DXC, Kappa, Germany) has been used to
detect and quantify fluorescent staining patterns [Arita et
al. 1992, Dunn et al. 1994].
Morphometric analysis
To access morphometrical data as well as the amounts
of bound antibodies (grey levels) a computerized image
analysis was performed with the GABA-ergic interneurons
of spinal cord and cerebellum (Imtron 2000, Germany) and
with the pancreatic Langerhans islets (Videoplan, Kontron,
Germany).
In several areas sized 541.000 tum? the cell density of
stratum moleculare et granulosum was determined.
Furthermore, the cell numbers of the endocrine por-
tion of the pancreas were measured and compared with
Tesults obtained from 2 healthy controls and 3 patients who
died with an insulin-dependent nonjuvenile diabetes mel-
litus. For this purpose, 5 um slices were stained with HE;
40 pancreatic islets were analyzed.
Results
Anamnestic findings
The disease of the 66-year-old woman started in April
1995 with neck stiffness and convulsions of her upper
limbs, which were followed by a slowly progredient dete-
rioration of her ability to walk. She sometimes tumbled and
could not stand up anymore without foreign help. In the
further course of the disease, muscle convulsions in proxi-
mal extremities and shoulders increased. No hints for an
epilepsy were observed. In addition, the patient suffered
from long-lasting insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and
strong arterial hypertony with peaks of 260/140 mmHg.
Clinical status, laboratory findings, and course of the
disease
During the clinical evaluation the following observa-
tions were made: strong lumbal lordosis and opisthotonus

(especially following external triggers and psychic ten-
sion), later a rigor-like increase of skeletal muscle tonus in
the extremities, strong reflexes, no pathological reflexes,
vegetative crises including tachypnoia, flashes. The latter
symptoms could be influenced by clonazepam administra-
tion. With time, the patient became weaker. EMG revealed
hints for a loss of interneurons in the spinal cord. Two days
before she died, a decrease of the renal filtration capacity
occurred accompanied by elevated sodium and potassium
levels.
During clinical and pathological examinations no
hints for a tumor were found. Standard laboratory tests:
GAD antibodies were detected in blood (7,000 U/ml) and
liquor cerebrospinalis (not quantified), negative results of
tetanus test (on animals), and microbiological tests for
clostridium species. Urine levels of adrenaline and norad-
tenaline were normal. No determination of autoantibodies
against amphiphysine was performed.
Macroscopical findings in the CNS
The brain exhibited an atrophy including weight re-
duction (985 g), cortical thickness of only 0.3 cm, and a
slightly atrophic corpus callosum. In the frontal slices
substantia alba cerebri and ventricular system were incon-
Spicuous. No alterations were found in caudate nucleus,
lentiforme nucleus, thalamus, hypothalamus, substantia
nigra and nucleus ruber, mammillary bodies, tractus me-
diales et laterales pontis. Normal morphology of cerebel-
lum and nuclei dentati as well as nuclei olivarii of the
medulla oblongata. The spinal cord preparation was 43 cm
in length and exhibited an acute hyperemia of the lep-
tomeningeal vessels.

Microscopical findings in the CNS
In all regions a high-grade edema of the CNS was
found. Hints fora beginning disturbance of circulation with
acute perivascular swelling of astrocyte branches were
observed. The blood vessels of leptomeninx and brain
exhibited a pronounced arteriosclerosis and arteriolos-
clerosis. Many corpora amylacea at the borderlines as well
as in the CNS parenchyma, pronounced lipofuscin accu-
mulation in many neurons of cortical layers II] and V and
in the basal ganglia. In the cerebellar cortex a distinct loss
of Purkinje cells was seen as well as demyelination in the
substantia alba of nuclei dentati and nuclei olivarii com-
bined with fibrillary gliosis in this area. In the cervical,
thoracal, and lumbal region of the spinal cord a pronounced
fibrillary gliosis (Figure 1) and many corpora amylacea
(dominating in the dorsal columns), and Schwann cell

Compared with a control brain, the cell density of
inhibitory neurons in the stratum moleculare et granulare
of the cerebellar cortex was diminished (Table 1). The
immunoreactivity of GABA-ergic neurons in the cerebellar
cortex with the GABA antibody was decreased (Figure 2).
A significant size reduction of Renshaw cells was
observed in the patient (Table 2). This feature was reflected
by a corresponding decrease of grey levels following im-
munostains with the GABA antibody (Figure 3).

Symptoms commonly associated with diabetes mellitus,
like elevated arteriosclerosis and hypertonia, were ob-
served. Her death was caused by repeated massive embo-
lism in the lung associated with some older rope-ladder-
like thrombs adhering at the walls of peripheral and central
lung arteries. A 3 cm sized infarct was visible in the right
lung.
Discussion
In the case of our patient dying at the age of 66 years,
SMS associated with IDDM was clinically suspected. This
was supported by the pathological and neuropathological
examination. The typical anamnestic and clinical signs
were already described by other authors [Giometto et al.

geet ASS
218 Warich-Kirches, von Bossanyi, Treuheit et al.
1994, Meineck and Richter 1987, Solimena et al. 1988,
1990, Tabira 1994, Vieregge et al. 1994) as well as the
characteristic neuropathological findings. A typical in-
crease of skeletal muscle tension, vegetative crises, GAD
autoantibodies, and hints for a loss of spinal cord in-
terneurons in the EMG, as well as a long-lasting IDDM
were found. In an older study [Whitley et al. 1976] a
neuronal loss in the substantia intermedia, selectively of
spinal inhibitory neurons, and a degeneration within dorsal
columns and tractus spinothalamicus have been reported.
To our knowledge, we describe for the first time alterations
in the cerebellum including a loss of GABA-ergic cortical
cells. In addition, Deiter’s nucleus, which contains cells
with the highest GABA levels of the CNS [Bourne 1972],
exhibited neuronal loss and cellular atrophy. In the spinal
cord a slight demyelination in the dorsal columns and a
neuronophagia of Renshaw cells were detected. Mor-
phometric analysis revealed a significant size reduction of
these interneurons. Langerhans islets exhibited alterations,
which can be seen frequently in long-lasting IDDM
[Cruickshank 1986]. An association of IDDM and SMS
has been observed by many authors [Pugliese et al 1994,
Solimena et al. 1988, 1990]. The autoimmune character of
SMS is furthermore supported by the fact that 22% of
patients carry the HLA allele DQB1*0201 [Pugliese et al.
1993], which is a susceptibility allele for IDDM and other
autoimmune diseases. But HLA typing was not performed
in our patient.
The diagnosis SMS is supported by the decrease of
cell density in the GAD-rich tissues like endocrine pan-
creas and stratum moleculare et granulosum of the cerebel-
lar cortex. In the latter, the alterations of the GABA-ergic
neurons have been demonstrated by 2 independent meth-
ods (cell counting and immunofluorescence studies with a
GABA antibody).
In several studies, GAD autoantibodies were ob-
served in up to 60% of SMS patients [Pugliese et al. 1994]
and sometimes they could be detected in both blood and
cerebrospinal fluid [Giometto et al. 1994] like in our case.
A tumor-related disease was excluded in our patient by
autopsy. Therefore, no test for amphiphysine autoanti-
bodies was performed. Amphiphysine [Lichte et al. 1992,
Yamamoto et al. 1995] autoantibodies have been described
in paraneoplastic SMS cases associated with mamma car-
cinomas [David et al. 1994, De Camilli et al. 1993] and
small-cell lung cancers [Dropcho 1996].
As described by other autors [Chang et al. 1995, Kuhn
et al. 1995, Meineck and Richter 1987] the symptoms
tesponded to the administration of clonazepam or diaze-
pam. Some authors describe a positive influence of immu-
noglobulins [Amato et al. 1994] or baclofen [Seitz et al.
1995, Silbert et al. 1995].
Our morphological data support the hypothesis, that
at least in a fraction of SMS cases GABA-ergic neutrans-
mitter systems play an important role in etiology. In the
sporadic form of the disease occurring during adult life,
GAD antibodies must be acquired during a long period by
autoimmunological mechanisms. Loss of GABA-ergic
cells may occur by T cell-mediated mechanisms similar to
the loss of 6B cells during IDDM [Lohmann et al. 1996,
Quinn and Sercarz 1996] and autoimmune reactions may
even influence GAD expression [Schmidli et al. 1996]. As
already proposed by Olafson et al. [1964], a low efficiency

of inhibitory spinal feedback mechanisms may participate
in the etiology of the disease. Hypersensitivity of spinal
motor neurons, caused by an insufficient inhibition of
Renshaw cells, may rely upon cellular atrophies and func-
tional impairment in that area, resulting in a decreased
secretion of GABA.
